On this page

Layered spheres and cylinders: the radial problem ​

Before this page

The Eshelby inclusion problem, whose uniformity result a layered pattern loses, and Concentration and contribution tensors, which defines the tensors such a pattern supplies to the Homogenization schemes.

A sphere or a cylinder made of concentric layers keeps its symmetry as long as its moduli depend on the radius alone, in the frame that turns with the point. Under a remote uniform loading, its problem then reduces to a few functions of . This page states that radial problem for LayeredSphere and LayeredCylinder together, and the two strategies that solve it:

  • radial modes and transfer matrices (section 3): in a uniform layer the radial functions are powers of , whose amplitudes are carried from one layer to the next. It is the method of Hervé and Zaoui (1993) for the sphere and of Hervé and Zaoui (1995) for the cylinder;

  • a system of the first order (section 4): the equations are written on the state that an interface transmits, and a layer is crossed by the power of a matrix, or by a numerical integration when its moduli vary.

Section 5 shows that they give the same transfer across a uniform layer, and which layers each one reaches:

LayerModuliCrossed by
uniform, isotropic (cylinder: or transversely isotropic about the axis)constantthe transfer matrix of its modes, or the power of a matrix
uniform, transversely isotropic about constant components in the local framethe power of a matrix
power law, PowerLawLayerthose of a reference, times the power of a matrix
graded, GradedLayerany function of a numerical integration

The modes and the matrices of each loading mode are on the two pages that follow, Layered sphere and Layered cylinder.

1. Loading modes and radial functions ​

In a sphere the moduli are given in the frame of the spherical chart, in a cylinder in the frame of the cylindrical one; the radial vector is the third of the first frame and the first of the second, and a field built by radial_ti knows which it is. A material that is isotropic, or transversely isotropic about , with coefficients that depend on alone, is unchanged by the rotations that leave the inclusion unchanged; so is, in a cylinder, a material transversely isotropic about the axis .

A uniform remote strain (a remote gradient in conduction) then splits into loading modes, each of which drives a field of fixed angular shape. Only radial functions remain unknown:

InclusionLoading modeFieldSize of the state
spherespherical part of   2
spheredeviatoric part of       4
sphere 2
cylinderin-plane dilatation and axial strain    2
cylinderin-plane shear    4
cylinderantiplane shear  2
cylinder across the axis 2
cylinder along the axis none

is the Legendre polynomial of and its derivative with respect to . The modes do not interact: each one is solved alone, and the tensors of the inclusion are assembled from their answers.

2. The state and its equation ​

The state of a mode at the radius gathers what a perfect interface transmits: the radial functions of the displacement, and those of the traction on the surface of radius . The traction is multiplied by ,

and, in conduction,    . The state is continuous where the moduli jump, which neither the derivative of the displacement nor the amplitudes of a modal solution are. Its size is twice the number of radial functions of the displacement.

Take the simplest case, conduction in a sphere, with a radial conductivity and a tangential one . With  , the flux      has the components

and its divergence vanishes when    . The first relation is the constitutive law along the radius, the second one the balance. Written on   , they are

Every mode of the table has this form. The first rows of are the constitutive law solved for the radial derivatives of the displacement, the last rows the equilibrium; holds the moduli at the radius and no derivative of them. The factor in front of the tractions is what makes free of when the moduli are. The matrices of every mode are built from the field equations, with symbols, in Layered sphere: the systems of the first order, symbolically and in its counterpart for the cylinder.

3. First strategy: radial modes and transfer matrices ​

In a layer of uniform moduli the equations of a mode are of Euler's type: each term has as many powers of as derivatives. Their solutions are powers , and a mode of state size has of them, the radial modes of the layer. For the conducting sphere,   gives    , that is   and    when  : the uniform gradient   and the dipole  .

The state of the layer is a combination of those of its modes,

holding the amplitudes and the columns of the states of the modes at the radius ; for the isotropic conducting sphere,

Eliminating the amplitudes between the two radii of the layer gives its transfer matrix,

Hervé and Zaoui (1993) carry the amplitudes rather than the state: at the radius between the layers and  , the continuity of the state reads    , and the amplitudes of the whole inclusion follow from those of the core by the product of the matrices . Both chains are the same products, cut at the amplitudes or at the states. The package cuts at the states, on which an imperfect interface acts (section 9), and which stay finite when a layer is incompressible.

The amplitudes are worth keeping: they give the field at every point of the layer, and its mean in closed form. This strategy is that of the isotropic layers of the sphere, of the layers of the cylinder that are isotropic or transversely isotropic about its axis, and of every layer in aging viscoelasticity, where the moduli are operators that do not commute and the order of each product is fixed mode by mode.

4. Second strategy: a system of the first order and the power of a matrix ​

In a layer of uniform moduli is constant. With   the equation is   , of solution    : the state is carried from the inner radius of the layer to its outer one by

No mode was looked for. For the isotropic conducting sphere:

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND, LinearAlgebra, StaticArrays
const RS = MeanFieldHomogenization.Core
const LS = MeanFieldHomogenization.LayeredSpheres

kᵣ = 3.0
M = LS._cond_system(radial_ti(SphericalChart(), kᵣ, kᵣ))     # k_\theta = k_r
2×2 StaticArraysCore.SMatrix{2, 2, Float64, 4} with indices SOneTo(2)×SOneTo(2):
  0.0  -0.333333
 -6.0  -1.0
julia
ξ = 2.0
Y_in = SVector(1.0, -3.0)                    # T̂ = r at r = 1: r q̂ = -k_r r
RS.radial_power(M, ξ) * Y_in, SVector(ξ, -3ξ)
([2.0, -6.0], [2.0, -6.0])

Let be the size of the state and    . The eigenvalues of come in opposite pairs: those of are symmetric about in a sphere and about in a cylinder. At size two,    with   , and the series of the exponential sums to

which holds for symbols as well. At size four the exponential of the   matrix is computed.

5. The two strategies compared ​

A solution    of     has    : the exponents of the radial modes are the eigenvalues of , and the states of the modes its eigenvectors. With the matrix of the eigenvectors and the diagonal one of the exponents, when has independent eigenvectors,

the transfer matrix of the modes is the power of the matrix of the system, written on its eigenvectors. For the conducting sphere:

julia
eigvals(Matrix(M))                                   # the exponents 1 and -2
2-element Vector{Float64}:
 -2.0
  0.9999999999999998
julia
Φ(r) = [r r^-2; -kᵣ*r 2kᵣ*r^-2]                      # the states of the modes r and r⁻²
r_in, r_out = 1.0, 2.0
Φ(r_out) / Φ(r_in), RS.radial_power(M, r_out / r_in)
([1.4166666666666667 -0.19444444444444442; -3.5 0.8333333333333333], [1.4166666666666667 -0.19444444444444442; -3.4999999999999996 0.8333333333333334])

The pages of the sphere and of the cylinder state the first strategy on  , without the factor , as the package carries it. With the diagonal matrix of ones on the displacements and of on the tractions, its transfer matrix is   , which the test suite checks for every loading mode of the sphere and of the cylinder.

What differs is what each strategy needs and gives:

Radial modes and transfer matricesSystem of the first order
needsthe exponents and the shapes of the modes, case by casethe matrix , read on the equations
equal or complex exponentsa modal solution changes form (, oscillating modes)one case: the power does not use the exponents
moduli that vary in the layerno modes in generalthe same system, integrated
closed formsat any size, with symbolsat size two; at size four through the eigenvectors
amplitudes of the layerknown: pointwise fields, harmonics of any degreenot known: the means are read on the states (section 10)
moduli that do not commute (aging viscoelasticity)each product in its ordernot available

The package therefore solves by its modes a sphere whose layers are all isotropic and uniform, and the layers of a cylinder that are isotropic or transversely isotropic about its axis. A layer transversely isotropic about the radius, a power-law or a graded one is crossed by the second strategy; in a sphere that holds one such layer, every layer is. An isotropic layer written as a radial one gives the same tensors to rounding (sphere, cylinder).

6. A layer that follows a power of the radius ​

Let the moduli of a layer be those of a reference, uniform, times . A matrix has the blocks

being the blocks of the reference: ratios of moduli stay, a compliance is divided by and a stiffness multiplied by it. The tractions of the state, divided by , give a state that obeys a system of constant matrix,

so that the layer is crossed by , exactly. In conduction the exponents are the roots of    , the classical result for a shell graded as a power.

julia
k_c, k_s, β, R, k₀ = 8.0, 0.4, 2.5, 1.6, TensISO{3}(1.3)       # core, shell, exponent, outer radius, matrix
exact = LayeredSphere((1.0, R), (TensISO{3}(k_c), PowerLawLayer(TensISO{3}(k_s), β)))
property_contribution(exact, k₀)
TensND.TensISO{2, 3, Float64, 1}
→ decomposition: (-0.019091282013223188) 𝟏

7. A graded layer: numerical integration ​

For any other profile the system     is integrated across the layer, in the variable from 0 to 1, by an explicit Runge-Kutta method with step control. A function given as the modulus of a layer is such a profile:

julia
integrated = LayeredSphere((1.0, R), (TensISO{3}(k_c), r -> TensISO{3}(k_s * r^β)))
property_contribution(integrated, k₀)
TensND.TensISO{2, 3, Float64, 1}
→ decomposition: (-0.019091282013548927) 𝟏

The two answers agree to the tolerance of the integration (reltol, abstol of GradedLayer). The integration carries real, complex and dual numbers alike: the complex moduli of a viscoelastic material at a frequency, and the derivatives with respect to a parameter of the profile or to a radius. An elastic zone with interfaces at given radii is solved in Graded isotropic layers with interfaces at given radii.

julia
using ForwardDiff
contribution(β) = TensND.get_data(property_contribution(LayeredSphere((1.0, R), (TensISO{3}(k_c), r -> TensISO{3}(k_s * r^β))), k₀))[1]
closed(β) = TensND.get_data(property_contribution(LayeredSphere((1.0, R), (TensISO{3}(k_c), PowerLawLayer(TensISO{3}(k_s), β))), k₀))[1]
ForwardDiff.derivative(contribution, β), ForwardDiff.derivative(closed, β)
(0.2917654152246984, 0.29176541522563804)

Uniform layers that follow the profile, as graded_layers cuts them, tend to the same answer as the square of their thickness:

julia
using Plots
profile(r) = TensISO{3}(k_s * r^β)
value(sphere) = TensND.get_data(property_contribution(sphere, k₀))[1]
ns = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
errors = map(ns) do n
    radii, moduli = graded_layers(profile, 1.0, R, n)
    abs(value(LayeredSphere((1.0, radii...), (TensISO{3}(k_c), moduli...))) / value(exact) - 1)
end
plot(ns, errors; xscale = :log10, yscale = :log10, marker = :circle, label = "n uniform layers",
    xlabel = "number of layers n", ylabel = "relative difference with the exact layer")
plot!(ns, errors[1] .* (ns[1] ./ ns) .^ 2; linestyle = :dash, label = "n⁻²")
hline!([abs(value(integrated) / value(exact) - 1)]; linestyle = :dot, label = "integrated layer")

8. The center ​

At the center the solutions that stay bounded are kept. With the modes of a uniform core, the amplitudes of those that are singular at   are set to zero. With its system, the regular solutions are the modes whose exponent has a real part above that of the pairs, : the eigenvectors of of eigenvalues of positive real part. Their span is the range of the projector

being the matrix that has the eigenvectors of and the signs of the real parts of its eigenvalues. At size two it is ; at size four it is the limit of Newton's iteration    . A mode has one regular solution at size two and two at size four; independent columns of are their states at the radius of the core.

In a graded core the moduli vary down to the center, where the profile must have a value. Carrying two regular solutions from a small radius does not work: both turn toward the one of largest exponent and the pair loses its second direction. Their span is carried instead, by its impedance , the matrix that gives the tractions of a regular state from its displacements,    . Inserted in the system, with the blocks of ,

a Riccati equation, integrated from the impedance of the uniform medium found at the center. The regular solutions being the growing ones, their impedance is the solution this equation is attracted to when increases, and the integration is stable.

9. Interfaces, the matrix, and the amplitude ​

The regular states of the core are carried outward: across a layer by sections 3 to 7, across an interface by its jump matrix , which acts on the state,    (sphere, cylinder). A perfect interface has  . A spring or a Kapitza resistance adds to the displacement a multiple of the traction, a membrane or a conducting surface adds to the traction a multiple of the displacement:

A layer of any kind may have any of them on its outer radius, and the chain is the same for the two strategies.

At the outer radius the states found are those of the inclusion up to amplitudes, being half the size of the state. The matrix is uniform, its solutions are its radial modes, and only those that decay, plus the uniform field of the loading, are present: more amplitudes. The continuity of the state at , across the last interface, is a linear system of equations, which fixes all of them per unit remote loading.

A loading that acts inside the layers as well enters the system as a second member. The axial strain of a cylinder is the only one; it is appended to the state, as the page of the cylinder shows, so that the system keeps its form; with the modes, it adds a uniform term to the radial stress of each layer.

10. Averages ​

The schemes need the mean strain and the mean stress of each layer per unit remote strain. With the modes of a layer they follow from its amplitudes; with its system no amplitude is known, and they are read on the states. Over a ball or a disc of radius , of outward normal ,

the second one because the stress is in equilibrium. Both are linear in the state at , and a layer is the difference of two balls or two discs. The mean stress of a layer is not the product of a stiffness by its mean strain, since the stiffness varies in the layer: it is read on the tractions.

The mean of the moduli over a layer, which the bounds and some schemes ask for, is taken over the directions at each radius and, for a graded layer, by a quadrature along the radius:

julia
LS.layer_property_average(integrated, k₀)        # volume-weighted mean of the conductivity
TensND.TensISO{2, 3, Float64, 1}
→ decomposition: (2.606368279784528) 𝟏

11. Scope ​

  • Matrix. The reference medium is isotropic for the sphere, transversely isotropic about the axis for the cylinder.

  • Numbers. Real, complex and dual numbers, nested, for every kind of layer. Symbols with the modes of the first strategy, at any size; with the systems, for uniform layers in conduction: the sign of a   matrix and the step control of an integration compare values, which symbols do not have.

  • A power-law layer cannot be the core, where its moduli vanish or are infinite. In a cylinder it is integrated as a graded layer.

  • Not available with layers crossed by the second strategy: the pointwise fields, the multipole expansion, and aging viscoelasticity.
